Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
cut off all contact with friends and family

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette: Arthur Vance was fifty-one when a sudden cardiac arrhythmia dropped him during a morning staff meeting at the high school he led for twelve years. He was rushed to the county hospital, where the emergency team's rapid response left him with a lasting imprint of the burning antiseptic on his skin and the heavy, chemical tang of industrial alcohol swabs against his throat. The weeks that followed were a blur of intubation, chest compressions, and the relentless hum of life support. Because his survival depended entirely on those precise clinical environments, the antiseptic and alcohol odors became inextricably linked to his own mortality. Now, the sharp alcohol scent in the staff restroom or the sight of a nurse's clipboard instantly pulls the trauma forward. That olfactory cue doesn't merely remind him of the event; it forces the fragmented images of the ICU to surface against his will, and the sheer physiological terror of that moment quickly convinces him that his body can no longer be trusted. The conviction that his physiology was fundamentally unreliable reshaped how Arthur moved through the day. Because he was certain he could no longer rely on his own cardiovascular stability, he systematically withdrew from situations that might demand physical exertion or unexpected medical attention. He began rehearsing every faculty meeting script in his head long before he entered the building, and he stopped returning calls from his late wife's siblings, claiming exhaustion. These rigid coping habits were his direct response to the negative self-evaluations that took hold; he believed only through extreme control and withdrawal could he prevent another collapse. Yet, his isolation and constant internal monologues soon fed back into his trauma processing. The more he rehearsed conversations and cut off his support network, the less grounded he felt, which in turn made the hospital smells and medical procedures in the school clinic trigger a fresh wave of dread. Arthur's memory quality dictated his daily reality. When he attempted to deliberately access the hospital timeline, he found the narrative fragmented and impossible to reconstruct, a gap that deepened his suspicion that his mind was failing him. This deliberate retrieval failure, combined with moments when the full emotional intensity of the arrest flooded his chest without any clear image, solidified his belief that he had become an unrecognisable version of himself. The very triggers that sparked these memories also dictated his daily routines; because the alcohol wipes and examination tables provoked such visceral disorientation, he instituted a strict policy of avoiding any district health screenings and delegated all medical-related parent communications. His maladaptive avoidance patterns, in turn, starved his cognitive processing of corrective evidence, which allowed his negative appraisals to fester and sharpen. When his self-evaluations grew sufficiently severe, they acted as a cognitive filter, pulling the most terrifying fragments of his medical trauma to the forefront of his awareness whenever he was alone. The cycle tightened relentlessly across the following months. Arthur's negative appraisals of his own fragility directly heightened his hypervigilance, causing him to scan every corridor for the scent of antiseptic long before his body could register it. Simultaneously, the bodily reenactment that accompanied his intrusive memories-the phantom stiffness of his hospital gown and the remembered pressure of the ventilator-drove him to further isolate completely, refusing even casual lunches with former colleagues. These compounding strategies only reinforced his conviction that he was fundamentally broken. The administrative duties that once anchored his identity now felt like minefields, forcing him to pace the linoleum hallways and check his pulse beneath his collar before entering any meeting. At fifty-two, Arthur Vance finally attended an intake session, hoping for relief from the suffocating loop, but terrified that seeking care would mean returning to the very medical cues that had once nearly killed him.
